node.label: Timothy Mitchell
node.date_label: 1988 Colonising Egypt · 1991 Colonising Egypt — paperback with new preface · 2002 Rule of Experts
node.description: Timothy Mitchell investigates colonial power through the organization of space, knowledge and everyday administration. Colonising Egypt studies nineteenth-century arrangements that made populations and places appear ordered and governable. He connects disciplinary practices to colonial settings rather than treating them as developments confined to Europe. Rule of Experts and Carbon Democracy extend his historical inquiries into expertise, political economy and energy. His work combines historical research with political theory; the selected connections here rest on his own paperback preface to Colonising Egypt.

incident_edges.relationship: Colonial power is examined through the production of ordered spaces and governable persons
incident_edges.evidence_note: Paperback preface ix–xi describes rural regulation, schooling and spatial partition; its historical claim concerns the power to colonise rather than a comprehensive narrative of British occupation.

incident_edges.relationship: Spatial organization becomes part of an inquiry into governing power
incident_edges.evidence_note: Preface x–xii links surveillance, enclosure and exhibitionary order with colonial power, and locates disciplinary experiments beyond Europe. The connection concerns this documented analysis, not universal adoption by spatial historians.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

named_group_routes.relationship: The Social in Question (2002) printed Latour's case for replacing 'the social' with 'association'; Joyce later named 'science studies' and 'the new materialism' as what he took up 'alongside' Foucault (2014); Koditschek read The State of Freedom as Foucault 'with an assist from Bruno Latour' (2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Moderate. Latour's chapter in Joyce's 2002 volume (read for 1.151, w3_latour_tarde_2002): ANT as 'a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word "social" in social theory to replace it with the word "association"'; Joyce's printing it is an editorial choice, and his introduction is unread. His own 2014 words (read in full) name 'science studies' and 'the various elements that make up what is being called the new materialism', with Timothy Mitchell as the example, not Latour. Koditschek (JBS 2014, read) names Latour: the book 'draws largely on the ideas of Michel Foucault (with an assist from Bruno Latour)'. The 2011 foreword (read): 'a new awakening of interest in the nature of materiality in relation to power'.

sources.title: Ian McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History,” Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (December 2000): 617–45, doi:10.3138/chr.81.4.616.
sources.citation: Ian McKay, “The Liberal Order Framework: A Prospectus for a Reconnaissance of Canadian History,” Canadian Historical Review 81, no. 4 (December 2000): 617–45, doi:10.3138/chr.81.4.616.

verification.note: Abstract read: the way past the "socio-cultural versus national-political impasse" is a re/connaissance mapping the Canadian state as "a project of liberal rule in northern North America", through which "liberal order became the national-political ‘commonsense’". Article body unread; McKay’s phrases on liberty, equality and property and on keeping liberalism and capitalism analytically separate (p. 629) are known here only through Fecteau (2009). Page range revised 2026-10-12 (answers Q20): cite 617–45. The DOI begins at 616 (the abstract page); Project MUSE reportedly gives 616–645; Crossref and OpenAlex give 616–678, a metadata error (their CHR 81:4 ranges overlap). End page not yet checked against a PDF. The abstract does not define liberalism by liberty, equality and property: that trio is Fecteau's paraphrase, not a checked McKay quotation. The best checked opening formulation is McKay 2000, 620–1, as quoted by Fecteau ('a certain politico-economic logic – to wit liberalism'). The 'cannot be conflated' line on capitalism is from McKay's 2009 reply (p. 385), not this essay. Checked against: Crossref DOI record (CHR 81:4, December 2000; Crossref gives 616–678 for the forum span); OpenAlex abstract (English and French); page range 616–645 as cited by Parnaby (2019); Crossref journal listing for CHR 81:4 (https://api.crossref.org/journals/0008-3755/works?filter=from-pub-date:2000-12-01,until-pub-date:2000-12-31); Project MUSE record https://muse.jhu.edu/article/590654 (blocked; page range reported by search summary). Checked against: Crossref DOI record; abstract via OpenAlex. The 1991 imprint is inferred from the McClelland and Stewart ISBN prefix and not separately checked. Checked against: 49thshelf book page (first published April 1991, ISBN 9780771086892; UTP reissue June 2008); Crossref DOI record (UTP 2008); review in Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), doi:10.2307/25143633. Same work also checked as crr_valverde_1991 (supporting_page_checked, 2026-10-12; cdn_religion_reform, cdn_religion_reform): Summary read: moral reform "was not the project of a marginal puritanical group but was central to the race, class, and gender organization of modern English Canada". Checked against: Open Library work OL1825719W; Crossref DOI of the 2008 reprint; OpenAlex summary. Addendum 2026-10-14: For the 1.135 person entry. The book's pages were not read. Wording is known from (a) in-period reviewers' quotations, read: Dehli 1992 (pp. 15, 17, 165), McCormick 1992 (pp. 9, 17, 42, 43, 90), Loo 1992 (pp. 35, 36, 41, 164), Wright 1995 (pp. 9–13, 41, 42, 43, 89–90, 98, 103, 166); and (b) Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 UTP reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C), whose page images were not viewable. The reissue keeps the 1991 pagination for the original text: the snippets put the reviewers' pp. 15, 17, 165 and 166 on the same pages, and the 1991 preface's p. 9 at p. ix (so 1991 p. 10 = 2008 p. x). Crossref chapter records: Preface ix–xiv; Introduction to the 2008 Edition 1–14; 1. Introduction 15–33; Notes 168–201. Snippet wording used: 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (p. x); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165); moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165); 'Marxist accounts (and in Canada this chiefly means accounts produced by the political economy school)' (p. 165); 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166); n. 33 (p. 171) cites Valverde and Weir 1988; n. 34 (p. 171): in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured'; n. 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis, 'Preconditions of the Canadian State'; p. 173: Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity'. The words before 'the term "moral regulation" from' on p. 173 were not visible. Acknowledgements (p. viii, snippet): 'Lorna Weir has been my best critic'.

sources.title: Tina Loo, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap and Water, Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 277–279.
sources.citation: Tina Loo, review of Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (Toronto, 1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 277–279. doi:10.2307/25143633.

verification.note: Read in full in the journal's PDF of the issue's reviews section (lltjournal.ca article 4867, galley 5740; pp. 277–279; signed Tina Loo, Simon Fraser University). Crossref gives Labour/Le Travail 30, p. 277. Passages used: the book is 'not a history of events ... but one of meaning' (p. 277); the reformers' allegories taught 'the right type of consciousness' (p. 278, quoting p. 41); 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift'; Allen's typology; 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'; private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (p. 278, her paraphrase); the state argument 'seems to be more asserted than proved'; she 'locates her book in the separate, but converging disciplines of history and sociology'; 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279).

sources.scope_note: In-period review by a historian (later co-author of Making Good, 1997).

sources.title: Mariana Valverde, “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State,” Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 213–222.
sources.citation: Mariana Valverde, “Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State,” review essay on Mitchell Dean, The Constitution of Poverty (1991), Jean-Marie Fecteau, Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989), and Gertrude Himmelfarb, Poverty and Compassion (1991), Labour/Le Travail 30 (Fall 1992): 213–222.

verification.note: Read in full (pp. 213–222) in the journal's own PDF (lltjournal.ca article 4860, galley 5733; citation line on p. 213: Labour/Le Travail, 30 (Fall 1992), 213-22). Passages used: 'a critique of political economy for its failure to theorize moral regulation and subjectivity generally' (pp. 213–214); 'moral capital of the poor' (p. 215); 'the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' and 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); Dean shows 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation'; 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism'; Dean 'undercuts the Marxist view that moral regulation is an unimportant offshoot of economic class relations by expanding the analysis of the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities pioneered by Corrigan and Sayer' (p. 217); Fecteau's study 'sadly lacking' Dean's awareness of gender (p. 220); n. 10 on Fecteau's essay in Colonial Leviathan and his perspective 'not to my knowledge otherwise represented in Canadian historiography' (p. 220); 'moyens de contrôle', 'a rather functionalist formulation', 'a model of negative class power', 'the pitfalls of marxist functionalism', 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital', 'a landmark work' (p. 222); thanks to Lynne Marks and Allan Greer (p. 222).

sources.scope_note: Her in-period statement of liberalism as moral regulation, and her critique of class-functionalist accounts of relief.

sources.title: Bruno Latour, "Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social," in Patrick Joyce, ed., The Social in Question: New Bearings in History and the Social Sciences (London: Routledge, 2002), 117–132.
sources.citation: Bruno Latour, "Gabriel Tarde and the End of the Social," in Patrick Joyce, ed., The Social in Question: New Bearings in History and the Social Sciences (London: Routledge, 2002), 117–132.

verification.note: Read in part for revision 1.151 in the author's typescript (21 pp.; typescript pages cited): pp. 1–2, 5, 7, 10. The author's page dates the essay 2001 and lists a German translation in Soziale Welt (2001). ANT is "a deliberate attempt at terminating the use of the word 'social' in social theory to replace it with the word 'association'"; "ANT actually has a forefather, namely Gabriel Tarde" (p. 1). "I must confess that I myself never enquired further than the dismissive footnotes of the Durkheimians" (p. 2). "Instead of saying, like Durkheim, that we 'should treat social facts as a thing', Tarde says that 'all things are society', and any phenomenon is a social fact" (p. 5). "Tarde can be said to have invented microhistory many decades before its discoverers" (p. 7). "It is not only the case that Durkheim has taken society as the cause instead of seeing that it is never more than a highly provisional consequence" (p. 10); the Durkheimians "have simply taken the explanandum for the explanans" (p. 10). Durkheim's position is given only as Latour presents it; Joyce's introduction is unread.
